# Percutaneous Left Atrial Appendage Closure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and rationale

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained arrhythmia, and its incidence and prevalence are increasing in the United States and globally. Its prevalence is expected to double by 2050 due to an ageing population, an increasing burden of comorbidities, greater awareness, and advancements in detection technologies. The dominant complication of AF is thromboembolic stroke, and the left atrial appendage (LAA) is the principal source: in the seminal surgical analysis by Blackshear and Odell, of patients with atrial thrombus, 91% had the thrombus located within the left atrial appendage [1]. This observation provided the anatomical foundation for mechanically excluding the LAA as an alternative to lifelong oral anticoagulation (OAC). Although effective, warfarin is limited by bleeding risk, narrow therapeutic index, and underuse; as with all procedures, LAAC is susceptible to complications, and there has been a contemporaneous introduction of direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) with more favourable risk–benefit profiles [2].

## Pivotal randomised evidence versus warfarin

The Watchman device was first tested against warfarin in PROTECT AF. Patients (n=707) with nonvalvular AF and at least one risk factor were randomized to either the Watchman device (n=463) or continued warfarin (n=244) in a 2:1 ratio; after implantation, warfarin was continued for ≈45 days, followed by clopidogrel for 4.5 months and lifelong aspirin [3]. After 2.3±1.1 years, the composite primary efficacy endpoint of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular death occurred at 3.0% versus 4.3% per 100 patient-years in the Watchman and warfarin groups, meeting non-inferiority criteria [3]. Longer-term follow-up reinforced this: in the final PROTECT AF report, the incidence of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular death was non-inferior with Watchman (8.4%) compared to warfarin (13.9%) [4].

The confirmatory PREVAIL trial was designed after a periprocedural safety hazard was identified in PROTECT AF. In PREVAIL the complication rate was low, but the warfarin cohort experienced an unexpectedly low ischemic stroke rate, rendering the efficacy endpoints inconclusive [5]. A pooled patient-level meta-analysis of both trials helped clarify the totality of evidence [6]. The definitive five-year analysis concluded that LAAC with Watchman provides stroke prevention in nonvalvular AF comparable to warfarin, with additional reductions in major bleeding, particularly hemorrhagic stroke, and mortality [7]. In a pooled net-clinical-benefit analysis of PROTECT AF and PREVAIL, the relative event profile differed by event type, since long-term warfarin therapy confers an increased risk of major bleeding events including intracranial hemorrhage [8].

For patients unable to take any anticoagulation, the ASAP study extended the concept: its purpose was to assess LAAC in nonvalvular AF patients ineligible for warfarin, since PROTECT AF only included warfarin-eligible patients who still received concomitant warfarin for six weeks after implantation [9].

## Comparison with direct oral anticoagulants

Because DOACs supplanted warfarin in clinical practice, head-to-head data became essential. PRAGUE-17 was a randomized noninferiority trial comparing percutaneous LAAC (Watchman or Amulet) with DOACs (95% apixaban) in patients with nonvalvular AF and a history of cardioembolism, clinically relevant bleeding, or both CHA2DS2-VASc ≥3 and HAS-BLED ≥2 [10]. In long-term follow-up, LAAC remained noninferior to DOACs for preventing major cardiovascular, neurological, or bleeding events, and nonprocedural bleeding was significantly reduced with LAAC [11].

More recently, the OPTION trial addressed the post-ablation population. In this international randomized trial of 1600 patients with AF and an elevated CHA2DS2-VASc score who underwent catheter ablation, patients were assigned 1:1 to LAA closure or oral anticoagulation [12]. The results showed that LAAO was noninferior to OAC for the composite of all-cause death, stroke, or systemic embolization and was superior to OAC for non–procedure-related bleeding [13].

## Device evolution and comparative performance

Iterative device development has improved closure and safety. The next-generation Watchman FLX was evaluated in PINNACLE FLX, which demonstrated improved outcomes and a low incidence of adverse events with the Watchman FLX device in a controlled setting [14].

The dual-seal Amplatzer Amulet was compared directly with Watchman in the Amulet IDE trial. The Amulet occluder was noninferior for safety and effectiveness of stroke prevention compared with the Watchman device and superior for LAA occlusion, though procedure-related complications were higher with the Amulet occluder and decreased with operator experience [15]. The investigator-initiated SWISS-APERO trial provided a second head-to-head comparison and, together with Amulet IDE, anchors current device-versus-device evidence [16].

## Device-related thrombus and residual leak

Device-related thrombus (DRT) remains an important concern. In the largest pooled Watchman cohort, among 1739 patients who received an implant, DRT was seen in 65 patients (3.74%) [17]. Importantly, nearly 75% of patients who develop DRT do not experience a stroke, and ischemic strokes in patients with DRT account for ≈10% of all ischemic strokes following LAAC [17]. Identified predictors include prior transient ischemic attack or stroke, permanent AF, vascular disease, larger LAA diameter, and lower left ventricular ejection fraction [17]. Peridevice leak is a related issue; in OPTION, at 12 months 20% of patients had a peridevice leak, compared with 10% in the PINNACLE FLX study [13,14].

## Guideline status and conclusions

Contemporary guidelines incorporate these data. The 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation provides recommendations to guide clinicians [18], while the 2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of atrial fibrillation were developed in collaboration with EACTS [19]. Both recognise LAAC as an option chiefly for patients with contraindications to long-term anticoagulation, framed within shared decision-making. In summary, percutaneous LAAC has matured from a feasibility concept into an evidence-based therapy that is non-inferior to both warfarin and DOACs for stroke prevention in selected AF patients, with consistent reductions in non-procedural and hemorrhagic bleeding offset by procedural risks and device-related thrombus that demand careful patient selection and post-procedural surveillance [20].
